To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the AKARI and BLAST data show the existence of a new population of dust in the Cassiopeiae A SNR, which is not associated with molecular clouds.

we have discovered new dust associated with the SNR that is too warm to be the interstellar medium, and we have characterized the cold dust emission from the surrounding molecular clouds and the SNR itself.

the dust in the Cassiopeiae A supernova remant is composed of at least three distinct dust populations: (1) a new population of tepid dust grains at 35 K, (2) a population of hot dust grains at 100 K, and (3) a population of cold dust grains at 16 K.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the interstellar medium (ISM) and its interaction with supernova remnants.
the study of the dust properties in the Cassiopeian A supernova remant and surrounding interstellar medium.
understanding the nature of the interstellar medium (ISM), the origin of the cosmic dust, and the evolution of galaxies in the early Universe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence for dust in the SNR, and that the dust emission seen at far infrared wavelengths is due entirely to the interstellar dust.

the dust in the remant is a combination of the hot dust in the SNR itself, the cold dust in the foreground clouds that are projected on the SNR and that are not physically related to the SNR, and a small component of tepid dust in the un-shocked supernova ejectae.
we find no morphological signature of the hot dust in the AKARI maps.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the AKARI and BLAST observations have revealed a new dust component in the Cassiopeian A SNR, and that the dust in the remant and the surrounding ISM is mixed together.

the AKARI data have revealed a new population of "tepid" (35 K) dust in the SNR and that the BLAST data have confirmed that the cold dust emission in the SNR is dominated by the foreground interstellar medium.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the cold dust emission is dominated by emission from the surrounding interstormellar medium and that any cold dust emission associated with the SNR is difficult to distinguish.
the SNR and the surrounding interstellar material are so intimately mixed that it is not possible to separate the two components at this resolution.
the dust in the SNR has a complex spatial and temperature structure that makes the interpretation of the dust emission challenging.
